name: Ginseng
subtitle: Panax ginseng, 50 vegan capsules x 800mg
standfirst: Ginseng root capsules made from Panax ginseng, a slow-growing perennial in the ginseng family, native to East Asia. Fifty vegan capsules to a pack, 800mg each, with no fillers.
body: Panax ginseng is a slow-growing perennial in the Araliaceae family, native to the cool forests of Korea, north-east China and the Russian Far East. Wild plants take years to reach a harvestable size, which is why most ginseng sold today, including this pack, is cultivated rather than wild-dug.

The listing calls the product 'Ginseng (Siberian)' in its title, while the text underneath describes Panax ginseng throughout. Those are two different plants. Panax ginseng is the Asian ginseng associated with ginsenosides, and Siberian ginseng usually refers to Eleutherococcus senticosus, a related but distinct species with a different set of active compounds. We have asked Reiss which one is actually in the capsule.
Each capsule is 800mg, and the pack contains fifty, with no fillers.
spec: Asian ginseng, Korean ginseng, Chinese ginseng
25 days on, 5 days off, as printed on the label
dose: Two capsules a day, in the morning or early afternoon, per the label.
supply: Fifty capsules. At two a day that is twenty five days, about three and a half weeks.
cautions: Not recommended in pregnancy or while breastfeeding.
Speak to your GP before taking this if you are on blood-thinning medication such as warfarin, or on blood pressure medication.
Speak to your GP before taking this if you have a hormone-sensitive condition.
If it disrupts your sleep, take it earlier in the day or lower the dose.

name: Chasteberry
subtitle: Vitex agnus-castus, 50 vegan capsules
standfirst: Chasteberry capsules made from the dried berries of Vitex agnus-castus, a Mediterranean shrub in the mint family. Fifty vegan capsules to a pack.
body: Vitex agnus-castus is a deciduous shrub native to the Mediterranean and central Asia, with slender grey-green leaves and spikes of small violet flowers in late summer. The berries ripen dark and peppery, which is where the plant gets its old country name, chaste tree, and the trade name monk's pepper.
The dried berries are what goes into the capsule. The listing does not print a capsule weight or an extraction ratio, so we cannot say how concentrated the fill is against the raw berry.
Fifty capsules to a pack, with the label recommending two a day, first thing, with water.

standfirst: Astragalus capsules made from Astragalus membranaceus, a perennial legume long used in Chinese herbal medicine. Fifty vegan capsules to a pack, 800mg each, with no fillers or bulking agents.
body: Astragalus membranaceus is a perennial member of the pea family, growing to about a metre with feathery leaves and small pale yellow flowers. It is native to northern and eastern China, Mongolia and Korea, where it has been grown as a field crop for centuries.

The listing does not say which part of the plant this pack is made from. Astragalus root is the part almost always used commercially, and the trade name huang qi refers specifically to the dried root in Chinese medicine, but we have asked Reiss to confirm rather than assume.

name: Gotu Kola
subtitle: Centella asiatica, vegan capsules

body: Centella asiatica is a small creeping perennial in the carrot family, with fan-shaped leaves on long thin stalks and tiny pinkish flowers hidden close to the ground. It grows in wet, marshy ground across South and South East Asia, and is eaten as a fresh salad leaf in Sri Lanka and Indonesia as well as dried for herbal use.
The leaves and stems, known together as the aerial parts, are the part most commonly dried for capsules, though the listing does not confirm this is what fills the pack, so we have asked.

name: Bugle
subtitle: Lycopus virginicus (as printed on the listing), vegan capsules
standfirst: Bugle capsules. The listing names the plant as Lycopus virginicus, a species usually sold under the common name bugleweed rather than bugle, which is more often the name given to a different plant, Ajuga reptans. We have asked Reiss to confirm which one is actually in the capsule.
body: Bugle is a common name with more than one owner. In British herbal use it usually means Ajuga reptans, a low, spreading plant in the mint family with blue flower spikes, common on damp woodland edges. In American and continental use, bugleweed usually means Lycopus virginicus or its European relative Lycopus europaeus, also mint family plants but a different genus entirely, growing taller and favouring wet ground near streams and ditches.

This listing's title says 'Bugle' but the body text names Lycopus Virginicus and calls the plant 'Bugleweed' throughout, which points to the Lycopus species rather than Ajuga. We have used the name printed in the listing text, but this is exactly the kind of common-name mix-up worth confirming before the page goes live.
The listing does not print a capsule count or weight for this pack.

name: Acacia Bark
subtitle: Acacia sp. (species to be confirmed), 50 vegan capsules
standfirst: Acacia bark capsules. Acacia is a large genus of well over a thousand species and the listing does not name which one this pack is made from, so the species is a confirmed open question rather than a guess. Fifty vegan capsules to a pack.
body: Acacia is one of the largest tree genera in the world, with species native to Africa, Arabia, southern Asia and Australia. Several are grown commercially for their bark and resin. Acacia senegal and Acacia seyal are the main sources of gum arabic, the hardened resin that seeps from cuts in the bark and is used as a food thickener and in traditional medicine across North Africa and the Middle East.

The listing describes the tree only as 'the ancient Acacia tree native to the Indus Kush region, stretching from North Africa through Arabia into India' and mentions gum arabic, which points toward Acacia senegal or a related gum-producing species, but no binomial is given anywhere on the listing. Because 'acacia bark' can mean the bark of any of dozens of commercially traded species, each with a different chemical profile, we have logged this as a query rather than picked one.

name: Chanca Piedra

body: Phyllanthus niruri is a small, upright annual herb, rarely taller than half a metre, with feathery rows of tiny leaflets along thin stems and seed-like flowers that sit directly under each leaf. It grows widely through the Amazon basin and other tropical and subtropical regions, often as a weed of disturbed and cultivated ground, and has a long history of use across South American herbal traditions.
